turns.content: Caesium-137 has a half-life of about 30 years. Convert this to seconds and calculate its decay constant in s^-1.
Use that decay constant to find the activity of a pure sample containing 10^17 Caesium-137 atoms.

From the rate just obtained, estimate the number of decays during 80 minutes and the corresponding number of emitted gamma rays. Use a gamma yield of order unity, and note how a yield of 0.85 changes the estimate.
A perfect 2 cm by 3 cm detector faces the pointlike isotropic source from 4 m away. Convert its area to square metres and calculate the fraction of the emitted radiation that it intercepts.
Combine the emission estimate with the geometric acceptance to obtain the number of detected events and its order of magnitude.
State which approximations make this an order-of-magnitude estimate rather than an exact count.
As a consistency check, verify the area conversion, inverse-square scaling, and the effect of using the 0.85 gamma yield.
Report the detected gamma-ray count to an appropriate precision and give its order of magnitude.
